newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh tribal repatriation ends uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh tribal repatriation ends uncertainty.

text.p: Bangladesh on Friday warmly welcomed tribal refugees returning home from India in an event which officials from the two countries said heralded a new era in bilateral relations.
Up to 50,000 tribespeople fled the Chittagong Hill Tracts to escape a 24-year revolt by Shanti Bahini guerrillas and a series of reprisal attacks on local tribes by Bengali-speaking settlers.
The Shanti Bahini want autonomy for the 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts, which borders India and Burma. They also want around 300,000 settlers expelled from the region.
More than 8,500 civilians, rebels and government troops have been killed in the insurgency, according to official figures.

Bangladesh government leader Abul Hasanat Abdullah, heading a party of senior civil and security officials to greet the first batch of refugees, said: "This is the start of a new phase in our relationship (with India),"
The refugees had walked over a bridge spanning the Feni river border into Bangladesh's Ramgarh township, 250 km (155 miles) southeast of Dhaka.
The refugees came from one of seven camps in Kathalchhari, a village in northeast India's Tripura state, across the river.

"I greet you," said Abdullah, parliamentary chief whip of the ruling Awami League. "It's your home and it's painful that you have lived in another country for so long. Today is a happy and memorable day for all of us."
"This (start of repatriation) has ended a prolonged uncertainty...and let there be no doubts that Bangladesh wants to resolve the Hill Tracts issues with all sincerity," Abdullah added.
Officials said 278 refugees from 64 families returned on Friday. A total of 6,700 are expected to return to Bangladesh by April 7.
The first to cross the wooden bridge on Friday was Oimala Bhikkhu, a Buddhist monk from Hill Tracts' Marma tribe.
"Peace is now prevailing in the Hill Tracts. It's time for us to go back," said Bhikkhu, who led six other monks to home.
"I only wish we don't have to come back to India again," said 27-year-old Roma Devi Chakma, mother of three children.
"It's a happy day for us, too," Upendralal Chakma, chief of the Tribal Refugees Association, said before the repatriation started.
"We believed the government in Dhaka would keep its pledge for proper rehabilitation of refugees," he told reporters at Kathalchhari in Tripura, 142 km (88 miles) south of state capital Agartala.
"The Hill Tracts problems are very old and needed a political settlement. Until that is found, I am afraid the problems will remain," he said.
Friday's ceremony at the border crossing also was attended by Tripura Deputy Chief Minister Baidyanath Majumdar.
"I wish the refugees a happy and peaceful return to Bangladesh. After the water treaty, this is another milestone in our historic cooperation," Majumdar said.
Bangladesh and India last December signed a landmark treaty that spelled an end to decades of enmity between them over sharing of water from the Ganges river.
Officials said the second phase of the repatriation would begin one month after April 7 so refugee leaders could visit the Hill Tracts to see if the rehabilitation was satisfactory.
Some 6,000 refugees were repatriated in February 1994, but the process was abruptly stopped without official explanation.

Upendralal Chakma on Friday accused then Bangladesh government of reneging on a 16-point agreement with the refugee leaders. "They violated the deal, made mockery of it and beytaryed our people," he said.
Abdullah said: "The repatriation suffered a setback because the past BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) government failed to keep promises and act sincerely."
"Inshallah, the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina will keep all its pledges. She is taking very bold steps in this respect," he told a farewell ceremony for the refugees at Kathalchhari.
Each returning family will get 15,000 taka ($350) in cash, house building materials and food rations for nine months, officials said.
